extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, natural science, sociology, and Victorian-era intellectual history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted programme and table-of-contents from Herbert Spencer's First Principles: a proposed multi-volume system of philosophy enumerating major Parts and their aims (The Unknowable; Laws of the Knowable; Principles of Biology, Psychology, Sociology, Morality, etc.). The page lists the intended scope and brief descriptions of each part/volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part I — The Unknowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Carrying a step further the doctrine put into shape by Hamilton and Mansel; pointing out the various directions in which Science leads to the same conclusions; and showing that in this united belief in an Absolute that transcends not only human knowledge but human conception, lies the only possible reconciliation of Science and Religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Part is to treat ultimate religious and metaphysical topics (chapters: Religion and Science; Ultimate Religious Ideas; Ultimate Scientific Ideas; The Relativity of All Knowledge; The Reconciliation). It frames the relation between religion, science, and the 'Absolute' and explains limits of human knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part II — Laws of the Knowable
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the ultimate principles discernible throughout all manifestations of the Absolute—those highest generalizations now being disclosed by Science which are severally true not of one class of phenomena but of all classes of phenomena; and which are thus the keys to all classes of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Part develops universal scientific/philosophical laws (chapters on Space, Time, Matter, Motion, Force; Indestructibility of Matter; Continuity of Motion; Persistence of Force; Transformation and Equivalence of Forces; Direction and Rhythm of Motion; Recapitulation, Criticism, and Recommencement; Evolution and Dissolution). One example generalization named is the Conservation (Persistence) of Force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology — Part I: The Data of Biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Including those general truths of Physics and Chemistry with which rational Biology must set out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames biological inquiry by establishing necessary physical and chemical facts and principles as the basis for biological induction and theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology — Part II: The Inductions of Biology
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the leading generalizations which Naturalists, Physiologists, and Comparative Anatomists, have established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes empirically-established biological generalizations drawn from observation and comparative study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology — Part III: The Evolution of Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerning the speculation commonly known as 'The Development Hypothesis'—its a priori and a posteriori evidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes the theory of organic development (evolution), weighing theoretical grounds and empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology Vol. II — IV: Morphological Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing out the relations that are everywhere traceable between organic forms and the average of the various forces to which they are subject; and seeking in the cumulative effects of such forces a theory of the forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examines form-development (morphology) as resulting from environmental and force-related influences; ties form to external conditions and cumulative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology Vol. II — V: Physiological Development
rubrics_metrics.description: The progressive differentiation of functions similarly traced; and similarly interpreted as consequent upon the exposure of different parts of organisms to different sets of conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats functional differentiation (physiology) as arising from differing exposures and conditions acting on parts of organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Biology Vol. II — VI: The Laws of Multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations respecting the rates of reproduction of the various classes of plants and animals; followed by an attempt to show the dependence of these variations upon certain necessary causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deals with reproductive rates and population multiplication, seeking causal explanations for observed variations (cross-references to prior essays noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology — Part I: The Data of Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating of the general connexions of Mind and Life and their relations to other modes of the Unknowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out psychological facts and how mental phenomena relate to life and the metaphysical 'Unknowable' established in Part I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology — Part II: The Inductions of Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: A digest of such generalizations respecting mental phenomena as have already been empirically established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes empirically-grounded generalizations about mental phenomena from observation and psychological study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology — Part III: General Synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A republication, with additional chapters, of the same part in the already-published Principles of Psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A synthetic account integrating psychological data and inductions into a coherent theory; indicated as a republication plus additions of previously published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology — Part IV: Special Synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A republication, with extensive revisions and additions, of the same part, &c. &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further synthesis focusing on special topics with revisions and additions to earlier treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology — Part V: Physical Synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempt to show the manner in which the succession of states of consciousness conforms to a certain fundamental law of nervous action that follows from the First Principles laid down at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridges psychology and physiology by showing how consciousness sequences follow nervous laws deduced from First Principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology Vol. II — VI: Special Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: As at present published, but further elaborated by some additional chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed analytical treatment of specific psychological topics, building on earlier published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology Vol. II — VII: General Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: As at present published, with several explanations and additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad analytic survey of psychological phenomena with clarifications and added material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Psychology Vol. II — VIII: Corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Consisting in part of a number of derivative principles which form a necessary introduction to Sociology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents derived psychological principles that serve as foundational background for sociological theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology — Part I: The Data of Sociology
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the several sets of factors entering into social phenomena—human ideas and feelings considered in their necessary order of evolution; surrounding natural conditions; and those ever complicating conditions to which Society itself gives origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lays out the empirical factors and contexts (psychological, environmental, self-generated) that must be considered in sociological study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology — Part II: The Inductions of Sociology
rubrics_metrics.description: General facts, structural and functional, as gathered from a survey of Societies and their changes: in other words, the empirical generalizations that are arrived at by comparing different societies, and successive phases of the same society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes empirically-derived generalizations about social structures and functions from comparative and historical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology — Part III: Political Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolution of governments, general and local, as determined by natural causes; their several types and metamorphoses; their increasing complexity and specialization; and the progressive imitation of their functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes governmental evolution, typologies, increasing complexity/specialization, and functional imitation as natural-process outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. II — IV: Ecclesiastical Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracing the differentiation of religious government from secular; its successive complications and the multiplication of sects; the growth and continued modification of religious ideas, as caused by advancing knowledge and changing moral character; and the gradual reconciliation of these ideas with the truths of abstract science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies the historical differentiation and evolution of religious institutions and doctrines and their interaction with scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. II — V: Ceremonial Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural history of that third kind of government which, having a common root with the others, and slowly becoming separate from and supplementary to them, serves to regulate the minor actions of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examines ceremonial or ritual governance as a distinct, evolving regulatory domain for everyday social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. II — VI: Industrial Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of productive and distributive agencies, considered, like the foregoing, in its necessary causes: comprehending not only the progressive division of labour, and the increasing complexity of each industrial agency, but also the successive forms of industrial government as passing through like phases with political government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies economic/industrial institutions' evolution, division of labour, complexity, and 'industrial government' analogies to political evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. III — VII: Lingual Progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolution of Languages regarded as a psychological process determined by social conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats language change as socially determined psychological evolution—links philology to sociology/psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. III — VIII: Intellectual Progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Treated from the same point of view: including the growth of classifications; the evolution of science out of common knowledge; the advance from qualitative to quantitative prevision, from the indefinite to the definite, and from the concrete to the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes intellectual development (science, classification, abstract thought) as social/psychological evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. III — IX: Aesthetic Progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fine Arts similarly dealt with: tracing their gradual differentiation from primitive institutions and from each other; their increasing varieties of development; and their advance in reality of expression and superiority of aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examines arts' differentiation and progressive refinement as part of social evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. III — X: Moral Progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibiting the genesis of the slow emotional modifications which human nature undergoes in its adaptation to the social state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies moral sentiment evolution as adaptive emotional change in response to social living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Sociology Vol. III — XI: The Consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating of the necessary interdependence of structures and of functions in each type of society, and in the successive phases of social development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explores interdependence (structural/functional) within societies and across developmental phases—how parts cohere and adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality — Part I: The Data of Morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations furnished by Biology, Psychology and Sociology, which underlie a true theory of right living: in other words, the elements of that equilibrium between constitution and conditions of existence, which is at once the moral ideal and the limit towards which we are progressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembles interdisciplinary empirical foundations (bio/psych/soc) necessary for moral theory and the concept of equilibrium as moral ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality — Part II: The Inductions of Morality
rubrics_metrics.description: Those empirically-established rules of human action which are registered as essential laws by all civilized nations: that is to say—the generalizations of expediency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes empirically-justified moral rules common to civilized societies, framed as generalizations of expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality — Part III: Personal Morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of private conduct—physical, intellectual, moral and religious—that follow from the conditions to complete individual life: or, what is the same thing—those modes of private action which must result from the eventual equilibration of internal desires and external needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develops norms for individual conduct derived from organism-environment equilibration and conditions for flourishing life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality Vol. II — IV: Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual limitations of men's actions necessitated by their co-existence as units of a society—limitations, the perfect observance of which constitutes that state of equilibrium forming the goal of political progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes justice as mutually-imposed limits necessary for social coexistence and as the equilibrium aim of political progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality Vol. II — V: Negative Beneficence
rubrics_metrics.description: Those secondary limitations, similarly necessitated, which, though less important and not cognizable by law, are yet requisite to prevent mutual destruction of happiness in various indirect ways: in other words—those minor self-restraints dictated by what may be called passive sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats non-legal, socially-required restraints (passive sympathy) that prevent indirect harms and protect common happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of Morality Vol. II — VI: Positive Beneficence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehending all modes of conduct, dictated by active sympathy, which imply pleasure in giving pleasure—modes of conduct that social adaptation has induced and must render ever more general; and which, in becoming universal, must fill to the full the possible measure of human happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats active, altruistic conduct (positive beneficence) as socially-adaptive behavior promoting generalized human happiness; positions it as moral ideal/goal.
